rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, two-year (2012-2013) center-pivot field experiment at Bushland TX comparing plant-feedback (IRT wireless sensor network, iCWSI thresholds) and manual (neutron probe) scheduling. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 3 report WUE and IWUE for sensor-controlled vs manual plots at each irrigation level; WUE within the same level was similar between methods, and Table 2 shows irrigation amounts similar at I75 but 15-120% greater for sensor plots at I50/I25. Q4: Section 2.5.2 and Fig. 4 measure the intermediate variable (canopy temperature / iCWSI) driving irrigation signals; Section 2.7.1 and Appendix Figs A.1-A.2 measure ETc by soil water balance and soil water content (no deep percolation). Q7: Section 2.4 states temperature data at NDVI <0.25 were unrepresentative of plant water status because of soil background, and Section 4 states early over-irrigation was due to false positive triggers from low canopy cover; conclusions restrict usefulness to the I75 and I50 levels. Q8: Section 3.3 notes solenoid mis-wiring in 2013 reducing analysis to 3 replications, greater standard deviation in plant-feedback plots, false positives from partial canopy, and Section 4 notes limitations from temporal frequency and cloudy days and failure to maintain 25% deficit level. Q9: Table 3 reports means <U+00B1> standard deviation for lint yield, ETc, WUE and IWUE by method x level.
rows.notes: The study's own result does not show an increase in CWP: WUE and IWUE were similar between sensor-based and manual scheduling at every level, and the sensor system applied more water (not less) at the I50 and I25 deficit levels, with the I25 target not maintained. It supports feasibility of sensor-based deficit control at I75/I50 with yields and WUE comparable to manual scheduling, not superior CWP. Single site, single soil, single crop, single field.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, two-year field experiment with randomized complete block design, hand-harvested lint yield from 10 m2 per plot. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 3 report lint yield for plant-feedback vs manual plots: similar at I75 and I50 in both years; significantly greater at I25 for sensor plots (141.8 vs 92.2 g m-2 in 2012) but with about twice the irrigation. Q4: Section 2.5.2/Fig. 4 measure canopy temperature and iCWSI (the stress signal driving irrigation), Table 2 irrigation amounts, Table 3 ETc, Table A.2 boll number and boll weight explaining yield differences. Q7: Section 2.4 states thermal readings require NDVI >=0.25 (adequate canopy cover) to represent plant water status; Section 4 attributes excess early irrigation to low canopy cover and restricts the method's demonstrated effectiveness to I75 and I50 levels. Q8: Section 3.3 reports 2013 valve mis-wiring reducing replications to 3, higher SD of yield and ETc in sensor plots, false-positive triggers; Section 4 notes further work needed for 25% level and limits from temporal frequency and cloudy days. Q9: Table 3 reports lint yield means <U+00B1> SD for each method x level in both years.
rows.notes: Yield was equal, not greater, than manual scheduling at I75/I50; the higher yield at I25 came from applying twice the water, so the study does not show increased yield under equivalent deficit irrigation. Overall method means (Table 3) show higher mean yield for sensor plots, attributed by the authors to larger irrigation totals. Single site, one crop and soil, field scale only.

notes: Full text appears complete. Both claim rows share one passage; the study is primary field evidence on sensor-based (plant feedback) scheduling but its results show parity, not superiority, in WUE and yield relative to neutron-probe-based manual scheduling, and over-application at deficit levels.
